title: The Oxygen Mix
intro: One problem, one session, 7,000 metres up. Nothing new — everything you built this unit, under pressure.

blocks.html:
Above 7,000 metres the air has too little oxygen to climb on. So the expedition carries blended gas: oxygen mixed with nitrogen, filled into a tank to an exact recipe.

A blend written 1 : 4 means 1 part oxygen to 4 parts nitrogen — exactly the kind of mix you were making in the Mixing Room, only now it keeps people alive.

You are on the gas log. Every single question below is the same four moves, in the same order:

read the ratio · count the total parts · find one part · scale it up.

blocks.prompt: Start with the tank in the picture. It holds 20 litres, blended 1 : 4.
blocks.hint: Count the total parts first — the picture has them drawn for you. Then one part is the tank shared between them.

parts.label: Oxygen (litres)
parts._working: Total parts: 1 + 4 = 5. One part: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 litres. Oxygen is 1 part, so 4 litres. The picture shows this directly — five equal blocks, one of them oxygen.

parts.label: Nitrogen (litres)
parts._working: Nitrogen is 4 parts: 4 × 4 = 16 litres. Check the whole tank: 4 + 16 = 20 ✓, and 4 : 16 divides down by 4 to 1 : 4 ✓ (simplifying, from the Mixing Room).

blocks.prompt: A bigger tank and an awkward-looking blend. 36 litres, blended 2 : 7.
blocks.hint: Nine parts in total. Find what one part is worth before you touch the 2 or the 7.

parts.label: Oxygen (litres)
parts._working: Total parts: 2 + 7 = 9. One part: 36 ÷ 9 = 4 litres. Oxygen is 2 parts: 2 × 4 = 8 litres.

parts.label: Nitrogen (litres)
parts._working: Nitrogen is 7 parts: 7 × 4 = 28 litres. Check: 8 + 28 = 36 ✓. Ratio check: 8 : 28 divides down by 4 to 2 : 7 ✓.

blocks.prompt: Now the real-world catch. Gas does not arrive by the litre — it arrives in cylinders. The oxygen cylinders hold 2 litres each.
blocks.hint: You already know how much oxygen each tank needs. How many 2-litre cylinders make that up?

parts.label: Cylinders for the 20-litre tank
parts._working: That tank needs 4 litres of oxygen (from x1). 4 ÷ 2 = 2 cylinders.

parts.label: Cylinders for the 36-litre tank
parts._working: That tank needs 8 litres of oxygen (from x2). 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cylinders.

blocks.button: Why some blends simply cannot be built ✨
blocks.html:
Here is a 24-litre tank, blended 1 : 3.

Four parts in total, so one part is 24 ÷ 4 = 6 litres. The tank needs 6 litres of oxygen.

But suppose the only cylinders in camp hold 4 litres each. How many of those make 6 litres?

One cylinder is 4. Two cylinders are 8. Nothing gives 6.

And this is not “I couldn't find it”. It is a proof. Every whole number of 4-litre cylinders gives a multiple of 4 — 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 — and 6 is not a multiple of 4. It is not there to be found. That blend cannot be built, by anyone, ever.

You have met this move before. In The Sequence Detective, the sequence 100, 94, 88, 82 steps straight over zero and never lands on it, because 106 does not divide by 6. Same sting, different costume.

Swap to 2-litre cylinders and the very same tank is easy: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cylinders. The tank was never the problem. The cylinder size was.

blocks.prompt: A 45-litre tank, blended 1 : 4. The oxygen cylinders in camp hold 3 litres each.
blocks.hint: Five parts in total. Work out the oxygen in litres first, then see how many cylinders that is.

parts.label: Oxygen needed (litres)
parts._working: Total parts: 1 + 4 = 5. One part: 45 ÷ 5 = 9 litres. Oxygen is 1 part, so 9 litres. (Nitrogen is 4 × 9 = 36, and 9 + 36 = 45 ✓.)

parts.label: How many 3-litre cylinders
parts._working: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 cylinders exactly. 9 IS a multiple of 3, so this blend can be built.

blocks.prompt: ★ Bad news from the supply run: the 3-litre cylinders are gone. Only 4-litre oxygen cylinders are left, and the tank is still 45 litres at 1 : 4.
blocks.hint: First test the 9 litres against multiples of 4. Then, for the second part: at 1 : 4 the oxygen is always a fifth of the tank — so what must the tank be a multiple of for that fifth to be a whole number of 4-litre cylinders?

parts.label: Can the blend be built? (yes/no)
parts._working: The tank still needs 9 litres of oxygen. Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12 — 9 is not among them, and 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 is not a whole number of cylinders. So: no, and it is a proof, not a search that failed.

parts.label: Smallest tank BIGGER than 45 litres that does work (litres)
parts._working: At 1 : 4 there are 5 parts, so oxygen is always tank ÷ 5. For that to be a whole number of 4-litre cylinders, tank ÷ 5 must be a multiple of 4 — so the tank must be a multiple of 5 × 4 = 20. Multiples of 20 are 20, 40, 60, 80; the first one past 45 is 60. Check: 60 ÷ 5 = 12 litres of oxygen, 12 ÷ 4 = 3 cylinders exactly, nitrogen 48, and 12 : 48 simplifies to 1 : 4 ✓.

blocks.html:
Last job, and the hardest thing in the unit. Now both gases come in fixed cylinders, and both counts have to come out whole:

GasCylinder size
Oxygen3 litres
Nitrogen5 litres

The quartermaster wants a blend of 2 : 5, filled exactly, with no gas left over and no cylinder opened twice. She does not care how big the tank is — she wants the smallest one that works.

blocks.prompt: ★★ Find the quartermaster's tank. Blend 2 : 5, oxygen in 3-litre cylinders, nitrogen in 5-litre cylinders, everything whole and exact.
blocks.hint: Seven parts in total, so the tank has to be a multiple of 7 before one part is even a whole number of litres. Try 7, then 14, then 21 — and at each one check BOTH gases against their cylinder size. Watch which gas is fussy and which never complains.

parts.label: Smallest tank that works (litres)
parts._working: Seven parts (2 + 5), so write the tank as 7 lots of one part. Oxygen is 2 parts, nitrogen is 5 parts. Test multiples of 7: tank 7 gives oxygen 2 (not a multiple of 3 — fails); tank 14 gives oxygen 4 (not a multiple of 3 — fails); tank 21 gives oxygen 6, which IS 2 cylinders of 3 ✓, and nitrogen 15, which IS 3 cylinders of 5 ✓. So 21 litres. Why nitrogen never complains: nitrogen is 5 parts, so it is always a multiple of 5 — exactly its own cylinder size. Only the oxygen is fussy, and it needs one part to be a multiple of 3. Checked by brute force over every tank size up to 400: the solutions are 21, 42, 63, 84 — all multiples of 21, with 21 the smallest.

parts.label: Oxygen cylinders used
parts._working: Oxygen is 2 of the 7 parts. One part is 21 ÷ 7 = 3 litres, so oxygen is 6 litres. 6 ÷ 3 = 2 cylinders.

parts.label: Nitrogen cylinders used
parts._working: Nitrogen is 5 parts: 5 × 3 = 15 litres. 15 ÷ 5 = 3 cylinders. Full check of the tank: 6 + 15 = 21 litres ✓, and 6 : 15 divides down by 3 to 2 : 5 ✓.

blocks.html:
🏔️ For the dinner table — a decision, not a sum.

The tank is fixed at 30 litres. The blend must be 1 : 3. The only oxygen cylinders in camp hold 4 litres.

First, show Dad it is hopeless — and it fails twice over, which is worth spotting. Work out the oxygen the tank needs and you will not even get a whole number of litres, let alone a whole number of cylinders.

So here is the real question, the one a climbing leader actually has to answer at 3am:

You cannot hit the blend exactly. Do you go slightly oxygen-rich, or slightly oxygen-lean?

Argue it properly. What goes wrong with too much oxygen? What goes wrong with too little, at 7,000 metres, four hours from the summit? There is no clean answer — which is why it is a conversation and not a calculation.

Then, if you want the sting in the tail: with only 4-litre oxygen cylinders and 6-litre nitrogen cylinders, which blends can you build? Try a few. (4 litres with 6 litres gives 4 : 6, which is 2 : 3. Two oxygen with one nitrogen gives 8 : 6, which is 4 : 3.) Is there a pattern in the blends you can reach — and one you will never reach, no matter how many cylinders you carry?

done.title: UNIT 3 COMPLETE 🏔️✓
done.html:
The Proportion Problem is solved. A ratio is parts, not amounts — so 2 : 3 and 4 : 6 are the same mix. You can simplify a ratio, share any total into one, find one part and scale it anywhere, and judge value by what one unit costs. You also know the thing most people get wrong: that some relationships look proportional and simply are not.

And today you did something harder than any of it. You proved a blend impossible — not unfound, impossible — using nothing but divisibility. That is the second time this course you have closed a door with a proof rather than a search, and it is the move real mathematicians get paid for.

Next: Unit 4 — The Modelling Workshop. Where the maths stops being given to you and starts being something you build to fit the world. Coming soon.
